course_description: The course will introduce students to the study of Islam, with a particular emphasis on Islam in the contemporary world. Students will benefit from learning about Islam in Australia and abroad, set against a background where Muslims have faced prejudice through the war on terror and Islamophobia. Students from a range of backgrounds will be challenged by the wider themes that the course raises that relate to human religious and cultural diversity in Australia and globally. The course covers a wide-ranging set of themes that include: ethics, science, media representation, gender, social inclusion and diversity, security, and free speech. This course may not run if there are fewer than 20 enrolments.

course_aims: This course aims at developing in students the abilities of independent research, analytical thinking, critical judgement, effective written and oral communication, and social understanding of the religion of Islam, Muslim communities and contemporary issues surrounding the two.ﾠ

learning_outcomes.description: Develop familiarity with the history, beliefs, and practices of Muslims and diversity therein
Develop deeper understanding of Islam as an historical tradition in diverse societies
Examine, discuss, and debate main issues related to Islam
Gain knowledge as to how the Quran and Hadith work to shape Muslim views and practices.
Develop a critical understanding around debates centering on Islam and Muslims
Demonstrate reasoned thought, creativity and a high quality of written expression
Conduct advanced research on Islam independently
Gain awareness of contemporary issues, such as gender and multiculturalism, with respect to Islam.

learning_activities.topic: Thinking about Islam In this introductory week we develop a framework for thinking about Islam, moving away from an approach that seeks to define an essence to religion, and encourage a way of thinking about religion that is embedded in local contexts and people’s everyday lives. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05

Dope Mipsters: Conceptualising Islam Scholars have rigorously debated: 'What is Islam'? This lecture provides a surveys key debates around conceptualizing Islam, and it daws on a case study of Muslim Hip Hop. We consider the influential work of Talal Asad's and his discussion of Islam as a ‘discursive tradition’. His conceptualization of Islam encourages a shift in thinking about Islam as a fixed set of texts, practices or social relationships, to seeing Islam as part of a field of debate and authorisation around what is ‘Islamic’ and what is ‘not Islamic’. Locating our understanding of Islam in an ongoing field of contestation and practice helps us to avoid essentializing Islam, on the one hand, and allows us to pay closer attention to themes of tradition, authority and how to account for change. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Representing Islam: Orientalism and beyond How is ‘Islam’ and how are ‘Muslims’ represented in academic and political discourse and in media? What difference does this make? Drawing on Edward Said’s concept of Orientalism, a founding text in postcolonial studies, we consider the importance of representation in history and in the contemporary context post-9/11. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07, L08

Science & Islam This week we explore the theme of Islam and science from an anthropological perspective, recognizing ‘scientific’ reasoning alongside religious reasoning and the ways in which religion and science interact in the everyday and the connections between Islam and modernity. We explore how Islam relates to local folk beliefs though healing practices and how religion and science connect to a transnational religious reinvigoration movement through the Turkish Gulen movement. The inquiry proposed moves away from standard theological and philosophical debates about the compatibility between ‘science and religion’ to examine how these relationships in everyday life and social and political rhetoric are conceived and what purposes they serve. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07, L08

Ethics and Piety What does it mean to be a ‘good Muslim’? This week we examine notions of Islamic piety and how people strive to live in an Islamic way and the challenges that often ensue. Drawing on questions of ‘everyday ethics’ on ‘how to lead a good life’ and cultivate virtuous dispositions and habits, we examine the seminal works of Charles Hirschkind on the acoustics of virtue formation (listening to cassette sermons) and Saba Mahmood’s examination of how wearing the veil serves as a means to inner transformation. We also examine the difficulties that people face in leading a good Muslim life, drawing on case studies from a high security prison (Williams) and a rural Egyptian town (Schielke). We also consider the meaning and performances of salat (Islamic prayer) and their personal and social significance across a range of contexts from Cairo to Indonesia. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L06, L07

Islam in Australia: Migrating and Adapting This lecture surveys the history of Islam in Australia, which predates the European colonial contact. It discusses the diversity of Islam and Muslims in Australia today and some challenges and opportunities. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L06, L07, L08

Islam and Gender The relationship between Islam and gender is an uneasy one from the perspective of secular-liberal politics and in consideration of feminist projects. Islam and gender conjures up associations with the subjugation of women and male patriarchy viewed as part of a ‘cultural backwardness’. This week we consider some case studies where gender norms are challenged, from an Egyptian mosque movement of women freely donning the veil in pursuit of piety, to gender roles in modern Iran and Muslim women in Malaysia starting a global movement for equality. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L06, L07

Midterm exam All students, including those completing the course by delayed viewing or by external mode, are required to complete the midterm exam in person . The exam will be held in week 8 and in place of the lecture. You must apply and receive approval for completing the deferred exam to be held one week later (see below). Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L06, L07, L08

Islam and Law In this lecture we look at Islamic law also known as Shari'a law as a legal system that has its foundation in the Quran and that has been practicsed by Muslims since the early days of Islam in the 7th Century. The implementation of Shari'a law by many Muslim-majority countries in recent decades presents a case for the incompatability of Shari'a law with contemporary social expectations. This lecture uses Malaysia as a case study to shed light into Islamic law evolultion, development and change paying attention to the legacy of colonisation on the type of Islamic law inherited by the postcolonial state and used to regulate citizenship, gender and religious life. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L06, L07, L08

You must attend the deferred exam date unless your original absence covers the period for this deferred exam (that is, you have an approved deferral period that extends longer than 1 week from the original exam date).
Public Holiday Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07, L08

Race, Ethnicity and Islam This week we examine how seemingly ready-made categories of identity, including nationality, ethnicity, and religion, are not static properties of individuals but are better thought of as emerging through relationships and processes. Through local contexts and examinations of everyday life we will examine how boundaries are formed and how national belonging, race, ethnicity and religion become entangled in complex and contested ways. We explore the case of white German converts to Islam and how national allegiances are questioned and ethnic boundaries are seemingly crossed. We also examine racialization in Australia and the UK and Blackamerican Islam. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06, L07

Mobilizing This week examines how Muslims have been active in seeking social change. We examine how Islam is related to broader social and political movements, before turning to more vexing issues around the relationship between Islam and violence. Using the literature from religion and violence, we seek to encourage broader thinking about Islam and violence in view of contemporary issues of terrorism, asking what definition of religion is assumed in the discourse around ‘religious violence’. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L08
